Statement: Antibiotics are medicines used to prevent and treat infections caused by bacteria.
Source_Org: World Health Organization
Source_Title: Antibiotic resistance - fact sheet

Statement: Antibiotics do not work on viruses. They do not treat colds and runny noses (even when mucus is thick, yellow or green), flu, or most sore throats (strep throat is an exception).
Source_Org: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Source_Title: Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do's and Don'ts; Antibiotics aren't always the answer (fact sheet)

Statement: Respiratory viral illnesses usually go away in a week or two without treatment; rest and liquids may help a person feel better while the body fights the virus.
Source_Org: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Source_Title: Antibiotics aren't always the answer (fact sheet)
Notes: Do not name specific symptom-relief medicines in the game.

Statement: Some infections caused by bacteria also get better without antibiotics, including many sinus infections and some ear infections. A health professional decides whether an antibiotic is needed.
Source_Org: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Source_Title: Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do's and Don'ts

Statement: An antibiotic will not make you feel better if you have a virus, and when antibiotics are not needed their side effects can still cause harm.
Source_Org: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Source_Title: Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do's and Don'ts; Be Antibiotics Aware - 7 facts (2020)

Statement: Different antimicrobials target different microbes: antibiotics for bacteria, antivirals for viruses and antifungals for fungi.
Source_Org: Frontiers in Public Health 2023 (WHO Europe KAB survey)
Source_Title: Knowledge, attitudes and behaviors on AMR among general public across 14 member states in the WHO European region

Statement: Only use antibiotics when they are prescribed by a certified health professional.
Source_Org: World Health Organization
Source_Title: Antibiotic resistance - fact sheet

Statement: Never demand antibiotics if your health worker says you do not need them.
Source_Org: World Health Organization; US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Source_Title: Antibiotic resistance - fact sheet; Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do's and Don'ts

Statement: Never share antibiotics with others or use leftover antibiotics.
Source_Org: World Health Organization; US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Source_Title: Antibiotic resistance - fact sheet; Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do's and Don'ts

Statement: Taking antibiotics prescribed for someone else may delay the best treatment for you, make you sicker or cause side effects.
Source_Org: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Source_Title: Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do's and Don'ts

Statement: Do not save antibiotics for later; taking the wrong medicine for a future illness may delay correct treatment and cause side effects.
Source_Org: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Source_Title: Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do's and Don'ts

Statement: If antibiotics are needed, take them exactly as prescribed and follow the health worker's advice; talk to a health professional about any questions or before making changes.
Source_Org: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; World Health Organization
Source_Title: Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do's and Don'ts; Antibiotic resistance - fact sheet
Notes: Deliberately avoids both 'always finish the course' and 'stop when you feel better' - see README (course-duration note).

Statement: Common side effects of antibiotics include rash, dizziness, nausea, diarrhoea and yeast infections; contact a health professional if side effects develop.
Source_Org: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Source_Title: Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do's and Don'ts

Statement: It is not acceptable to use antibiotics given to a friend or family member for the same illness, or to buy or request the same antibiotics because they helped with the same symptoms before (WHO survey answer key: both 'false').
Source_Org: World Health Organization
Source_Title: Antibiotic resistance: multi-country public awareness survey (2015), incl. Annex questionnaire

Statement: India's 'Medicines with the Red Line' campaign (Ministry of Health, Feb 2016): a vertical red line on a medicine pack, including many antibiotics, means it should be taken only with a doctor's prescription.
Source_Org: Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, India (via peer-reviewed review); Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, India (reported by Medical Dialogues, Mar 2025)
Source_Title: The role of Schedule H1 and Red Line campaign in improving antibiotic use in India. J Family Med Prim Care 2022;11(6):2656-61; Health Ministry launches Red Line campaign to curb antibiotic misuse

Statement: In India, antibiotics fall under Schedule H/H1 of the Drugs Rules, 1945 and are meant to be sold only on the prescription of a Registered Medical Practitioner.
Source_Org: Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, India (reported by Medical Dialogues, Mar 2025)
Source_Title: Health Ministry launches Red Line campaign to curb antibiotic misuse
Notes: Use only as 'meant to be sold on prescription' - no schedule names in-game.

Statement: Dispose of unused or expired medicines safely, for example through drug take-back programmes; ask a pharmacist how to discard leftover medicines.
Source_Org: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Source_Title: Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do's and Don'ts

Statement: Preventing infections reduces how often antibiotics are used and the likelihood that resistance develops; handwashing also helps prevent infection with germs that are already resistant.
Source_Org: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Source_Title: Show Me the Science - Why Wash Your Hands?

Statement: Wash hands with soap and clean running water, scrubbing for at least 20 seconds; if soap and water are unavailable, use a hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol.
Source_Org: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Source_Title: Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do's and Don'ts; Hand Hygiene Frequently Asked Questions

Statement: Handwashing can prevent about 30% of diarrhoea-related sicknesses and about 20% of respiratory infections such as colds.
Source_Org: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Source_Title: Show Me the Science - Why Wash Your Hands?

Statement: Cover your mouth and nose with a tissue when coughing or sneezing, stay home when sick, avoid touching eyes, nose and mouth with unwashed hands, and avoid close contact with people who have colds.
Source_Org: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Source_Title: Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do's and Don'ts

Statement: Getting recommended vaccines (for example, the flu vaccine) helps people stay healthy and prevents infections, reducing the need for antibiotics.
Source_Org: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Source_Title: Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do's and Don'ts; Be Antibiotics Aware - 7 facts (2020)

Statement: Baby wipes are not designed to remove germs and do not reliably clean hands; CDC does not recommend them for hand hygiene.
Source_Org: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Source_Title: Hand Hygiene Frequently Asked Questions

Statement: Lack of access to clean water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) and poor infection prevention in homes, health facilities and farms contribute to the emergence and spread of AMR.
Source_Org: World Health Organization
Source_Title: Antimicrobial resistance - fact sheet

Statement: Antibiotic resistance happens when bacteria change and become resistant to the antibiotics used to treat them. Bacteria - not humans or animals - become resistant.
Source_Org: World Health Organization
Source_Title: WHO multi-country survey reveals widespread public misunderstanding about antibiotic resistance (16 Nov 2015)

Statement: The misuse and overuse of antimicrobials in humans, animals and plants are the main drivers of drug-resistant pathogens.
Source_Org: World Health Organization
Source_Title: Antimicrobial resistance - fact sheet

Statement: Anyone, of any age, in any country can get an antibiotic-resistant infection; it is not only a problem for people who take antibiotics regularly.
Source_Org: World Health Organization
Source_Title: WHO multi-country survey reveals widespread public misunderstanding about antibiotic resistance (16 Nov 2015)

Statement: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria can spread from person to person (WHO survey answer key: 'true').
Source_Org: World Health Organization
Source_Title: Antibiotic resistance: multi-country public awareness survey (2015), incl. Annex questionnaire

Statement: AMR makes infections harder to treat and makes medical procedures such as surgery, caesarean sections and cancer chemotherapy much riskier.
Source_Org: World Health Organization; World Health Organization
Source_Title: WHO warns of widespread resistance to common antibiotics worldwide - GLASS report 2025 (13 Oct 2025); Antibiotic resistance - fact sheet

Statement: When first-line antibiotics stop working, more expensive last-resort medicines are needed; these are costly, harder to access and often unavailable in low- and middle-income countries. Resistance also means longer hospital stays and more deaths.
Source_Org: World Health Organization; World Health Organization
Source_Title: Antibiotic resistance - fact sheet; WHO warns of widespread resistance to common antibiotics worldwide - GLASS report 2025 (13 Oct 2025)

Statement: Any time antibiotics are used they can cause side effects and lead to antibiotic resistance; taking antibiotics creates resistant bacteria.
Source_Org: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Source_Title: Be Antibiotics Aware - 7 facts (2020)

Statement: In 2021 bacterial AMR directly caused an estimated 1.14 million deaths and was associated with 4.71 million deaths worldwide.
Source_Org: GRAM Project (IHME & University of Oxford), The Lancet 2024
Source_Title: Global burden of bacterial AMR 1990-2021 with forecasts to 2050. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(24)01867-1

Statement: GRAM forecasts more than 39 million deaths directly due to AMR between 2025 and 2050, with the highest burden in South Asia (about 11.8 million), which includes India.
Source_Org: GRAM Project (IHME & University of Oxford), The Lancet 2024
Source_Title: Global burden of bacterial AMR 1990-2021 with forecasts to 2050. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(24)01867-1

Statement: WHO's Global Antibiotic Resistance Surveillance Report 2025: about 1 in 6 lab-confirmed bacterial infections worldwide in 2023 were resistant; in the South-East Asia (incl. India) and Eastern Mediterranean regions about 1 in 3 were resistant.
Source_Org: World Health Organization
Source_Title: WHO warns of widespread resistance to common antibiotics worldwide - GLASS report 2025 (13 Oct 2025)

Statement: WHO 2015 survey: 75% of Indian respondents wrongly thought colds and flu can be treated with antibiotics (64% across 12 countries); 76% overall thought resistance means the body becomes resistant.
Source_Org: World Health Organization; World Health Organization
Source_Title: WHO multi-country survey reveals widespread public misunderstanding about antibiotic resistance (16 Nov 2015); Antibiotic resistance: multi-country public awareness survey (2015), incl. Annex questionnaire
Notes: Also a baseline-awareness statistic for the Background slide.

Statement: AMR is a One Health problem: the health of people, animals, plants and the environment is connected. WAAW 2026 theme: 'One Health, one action: Prevent AMR now'; the Global Action Plan on AMR 2026-2036 includes minimising environmental pollution from antimicrobial residues.
Source_Org: World Health Organization
Source_Title: World AMR Awareness Week 2026

Statement: Antibiotics should be given to animals only under veterinary supervision and not used for growth promotion or to prevent disease in healthy animals.
Source_Org: World Health Organization
Source_Title: Antibiotic resistance - fact sheet

Statement: World AMR Awareness Week (WAAW) is observed every year from 18 to 24 November.
Source_Org: World Health Organization
Source_Title: World AMR Awareness Week 2026

Statement: India launched its second National Action Plan on AMR (NAP-AMR 2.0) for 2025-2029 on 18 November 2025; the first plan covered 2017-2021.
Source_Org: Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, India (reported by Down To Earth, Nov 2025)
Source_Title: WAAW 2025: India's second National Action Plan on AMR released

Statement: Some bacterial infections, such as urinary tract (bladder) infections and skin or wound infections, can be treated with antibiotics when a health professional prescribes them (WHO survey answer key).
Source_Org: World Health Organization
Source_Title: Antibiotic resistance: multi-country public awareness survey (2015), incl. Annex questionnaire
Notes: Educational only - no diagnosis or drug names.

Statement: Key times to wash hands include before eating, after using the toilet and after blowing your nose, coughing or sneezing.
Source_Org: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Source_Title: About Handwashing / When and How to Wash Your Hands
Notes: Reviewer: confirm wording against the live CDC page.
